opus-5.5.text:
I think what's really exciting about mathematics is that it's one of the very few domains where you have a perfect verifier. When a model produces a proof, and you formalize it in something like Lean, you know with certainty whether it's correct or not. There's no ambiguity, no human rater disagreeing, no reward hacking in the usual sense. That's an incredibly powerful property when you're trying to build systems that get better on their own.

If you think about how self-improvement works in practice, the bottleneck is almost always the quality of the feedback signal. In most domains, you're relying on human preferences or learned reward models, and those are noisy and can be gamed. In math, the system can attempt a problem, generate thousands of candidate solutions, check them all with a formal verifier, and then train on the ones that are actually correct. And then it can do that again, on harder problems, and again. The loop closes cleanly.

The other thing I find compelling is that mathematics is essentially unbounded in difficulty. You're never going to run out of harder problems. There's this whole frontier of open conjectures, and below that a huge landscape of intermediate results. So you have a natural curriculum that stretches as far as you want it to go.

And then there's the broader picture: mathematical reasoning underlies so much else. Software verification, hardware design, physics, anything where correctness really matters. If you can build a system that reasons rigorously and gets better at it on its own, that capability starts to transfer to all these other areas where we really care that the answer is right, not just plausible. So to me math isn't just a nice sandbox. It's kind of the foundation for building AI we can actually trust.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The thing that excites me most about math is that it's the one domain where the feedback loop can actually close without a human in it. In most fields, if a model produces something, you need a person to check whether it's right, and that person becomes the bottleneck. In math, if you write a proof in a formal system like Lean, a tiny verifier can check it, and the answer is binary. Either it compiles or it doesn't. There's no ambiguity, no grader with opinions, no reward model you can fool.

That property is what makes recursive improvement possible. The model can generate thousands of attempts at a problem, and every success is a perfectly labeled training example, and every failure is a perfectly labeled negative. You can turn compute into supervision at essentially unlimited scale. And unlike a lot of synthetic data, you know it's not polluted, because the verifier won't accept something that's wrong.

The second thing is that math is unbounded in difficulty. With a lot of benchmarks, you saturate them and then you have to go find a harder dataset. In math, the model can keep proposing new conjectures, keep trying to prove them, and the frontier just moves. It's a domain where the problem supply doesn't run out.

And then the part people underrate is that mathematical reasoning is really just a very pure form of general reasoning. The skills you build when a system learns to decompose a hard theorem into lemmas, figure out which ones are tractable, back up when a path isn't working, and manage a long chain of dependencies, those transfer. We see that already. So I think of math less as a niche application and more as the cleanest possible training ground for the kind of long-horizon, verifiable reasoning you want everywhere else, including in software and science.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is that mathematics gives you a way to check whether you’re actually making progress. A problem can be incredibly hard to solve, but once you have a formal proof, you can check it mechanically. So you have a source of feedback that doesn’t depend on a human judging whether an answer sounds convincing.

That creates a really interesting loop: a model can attempt problems, get feedback on its proofs, and use successful attempts as training data to improve. The difficult part is making sure that loop produces new capabilities, rather than just more examples of things the model already knows how to do.

And mathematics is open-ended. You can move from solving individual problems to discovering useful lemmas and abstractions that make whole classes of problems easier. That’s the possibility I find exciting: a system that helps build the tools for its own next step.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is that mathematics gives you a way to check whether you’re actually making progress. You can generate a proof, and if you express it formally, a proof checker can tell you whether it’s correct. That’s a powerful feedback signal for a system that’s trying to improve itself.

And mathematics has this natural structure where solving one problem gives you tools for solving others. You prove a lemma, and now that lemma becomes a building block. So you can imagine a loop where a model proposes problems, tries to solve them, verifies the solutions, and learns from that experience. The interesting question is whether that loop can keep producing useful new challenges, rather than just getting better at things it already knows how to do.
